question: Can the full study be done, and how?

eldridge2016.cite: Eldridge et al. (2016). CONSORT 2010 statement: extension to randomised pilot and feasibility trials. BMJ 355: i5239.
eldridge2016.checked: every quote read word for word in the vault's text copy (library No. 287) on 20 Nov 2026; the article is online-only (i5239), so places are given as its introduction, box 1 and checklist items; in-text reference numbers are left out

steps.title: Ask about feasibility
steps.text: Name what is uncertain about the future main study: recruitment, retention, delivery, measurement. Those are the pilot's questions.

quotes.text: a feasibility study for a future definitive RCT asks whether the future trial can be done, should be done, and, if so, how.
The rationale of a pilot trial is to investigate areas of uncertainty about the future definitive RCT

steps.title: Set criteria first
steps.text: Before starting, write down what result means go, go with changes, or stop.

quotes.text: This might involve formal progression criteria to decide whether to proceed, to proceed with amendments, or not to proceed

steps.title: Size for feasibility
steps.text: Choose the number of participants to answer the feasibility questions, and say why.

quotes.text: The number of participants in a pilot study should be based on the feasibility objectives and some rationale should be given

steps.title: Rehearse small
steps.text: Run the main study, or part of it, on a small scale, and count everyone at every stage.

quotes.text: in a pilot study (that might or might not be randomised) the future definitive RCT, or part of it, is conducted on a smaller scale.
the numbers of participants who were approached and/or assessed for eligibility, randomly assigned, received intended treatment, and were assessed for each objective

steps.title: Decide, don't test
steps.text: Judge the counts against the criteria and decide on the main study. Do not test whether the treatment works: the pilot is too small for that.

quotes.text: Formal hypothesis testing for effectiveness (or efficacy) is not recommended.

low-power.text: The aim of a pilot trial is not to assess effectiveness (or efficacy) and it will usually be underpowered to do this

limits: Eldridge et al. (2016) is written for randomised pilot trials; non-randomised pilots follow the same logic but are not covered by the guideline.
